reason: The Provisioned concurrency bullet of the decision guide says it keeps a specified number of instances warm, reduces cold start latency, increases costs, and you pay even when instances are not handling requests.
The note says an event source must point to the correct alias or version, otherwise the function won't use provisioned concurrency environments; the claim restates it.
Under Provisioned Concurrency Pricing, execution beyond the configured concurrency is billed at the rate in the main AWS Lambda Pricing section, which is the on-demand function rate.
The pricing page says verbatim that the Lambda free tier does not apply to functions enabling Provisioned Concurrency.
The quote states both parts: no cold start behavior because the environment is prepared ahead, and provisioned concurrency must apply to a specific version or alias, not $LATEST.

Example 1 under Provisioned Concurrency Pricing gives $0.0000041667 per GB-s, followed by separate request and duration charges; the page states all examples there use US East (N. Virginia) prices (www/lambda/pricing line 177).
The quote states you pay for the concurrency configured and the period configured, plus requests and duration when enabled and executed.
The quote states the time from enable to disable, rounded up to the nearest five minutes, with price depending on memory and configured concurrency.
The best-practices quote defines provisioned concurrency as pre-initialized environments, used when available, and says Lambda can scale above and beyond the setting if required.

Example 1 (mobile backend, x86) gives $0.0000166667 per GB-s monthly compute price with 400,000 GB-s free tier; the line above the example says examples use US East (N. Virginia) prices (www/lambda/pricing line 111).
The same example gives $0.20 per one million requests; the examples are stated to use US East (N. Virginia) prices (www/lambda/pricing line 111).
Under Lambda Functions Pricing the quote states pricing by requests served and duration in GB-seconds, and memory chosen with proportional CPU.
The quote says the first pricing tier is, for example, up to 6 billion GB-seconds per month in US East (Ohio); the claim keeps the Ohio example scope.
The quote states tiers apply to aggregate monthly duration on the same architecture, same Region, within the account, or across the organization's accounts with consolidated billing.
The quotas table row Execution processes/threads gives 1,024, and Lambda Managed Instances use Bottlerocket default limits.
The quote says provisioned concurrency is not online immediately, allocation starts after a minute or two, and up to 6,000 environments per minute per function.
The quote says provisioned concurrency counts towards the account concurrency limit and that configuring it incurs charges.
The quotas row gives 10 x allocated provisioned concurrency requests per second per version or alias, applying only to functions with provisioned concurrency.
The note says verbatim you can't allocate more provisioned concurrency than reserved concurrency for a function.
The Important note says put-resource-policy replaces the existing policy and overwrites add-permission permissions; the update section says add-permission adds a statement without overwriting.
The quote says for queue event source mappings, time between retries and failed-event destination come from the source queue's visibility timeout and redrive policy.
The quote states concurrent execution and storage quotas apply per Region, and ENI quotas per VPC regardless of Region.
The quote states service quotas consist of hard limits you cannot change and soft limits you can request increases for.
The Scaling characteristics bullet says RDS has fixed capacity based on instance size and simultaneous Lambda connections might exceed the connection quota.
The quote states Amazon RDS charges an hourly rate for proxies based on the database instance size.
The page opens with direct or proxy connections; direct for simple scenarios, proxies recommended for production, and a proxy pools shared connections to reach high concurrency.
The two quotes state: no X-Ray active tracing needed, on by default for all customers, no charge, stops and notifies by default, and a function can be configured to allow recursion.
The quote states approximately 16 invocations in one chain stops the next invocation and notifies you; other triggers are not affected.
The quotes state detection only for certain supported services with a supported SDK, list SQS, S3, SNS and EventBridge custom event buses, and include loops of only Lambda functions.
The quote states unintended loops can cause unexpected charges and can make Lambda scale and use all available account concurrency.

The programming-model list (introduced by scaling through more instances) says requests might be processed out of order or concurrently and state should be stored elsewhere; the 'unless noted otherwise' condition is kept in the qualifiers.
The quote states the remaining 100 units are for functions without reserved concurrency and that with a 1,000 limit you cannot reserve all 1,000 to one function.
Under Concurrency quotas, the quote says at the function level you can reserve up to 900 units across all functions by default.
The quote says verbatim that configuring reserved concurrency incurs no additional charges.
The quote says to intentionally throttle, set reserved concurrency to 0, which stops processing events until the limit is removed.
The note says with reserved concurrency zero on an async function, new events go to the configured DLQ or on-failure destination without retries.
The quotes state resource-based policies grant other accounts, users, organizations and AWS services access, and each statement's Resource is the function, version or alias.
The quotas table row Function resource-based policy gives 20 KB.

The quotes cover Max Memory Used analysis and the Power Tuning recommendation; the paragraph just above (best-practices line 53) says memory usage is viewed in Amazon CloudWatch with a REPORT entry per invoke.
Under Concurrency quotas, the quote states at both account and function level a requests per second limit equal to 10 times the concurrency quota.
